messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
**Standard error of the sample mean (the “standard deviation” of the null‑hypothesis sampling distribution)**  

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]

where  
- \(s = 1.4\) (sample standard deviation)  
- \(n = 40\) (sample size)

\[
SE = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}} = \frac{1.4}{6.3249} \approx 0.2215
\]

So the standard deviation of the null‑hypothesis test (i.e., the standard error of the mean under the null) is **≈ 0.22**.
message.reasoning:
The user says: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6."

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? That likely refers to the standard error of the mean under null hypothesis? The standard error is sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). But they might want the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under null hypothesis. That is sigma/sqrt(n). They gave sample_std_dev=1.4, sample_size=40. So standard error = 1.4 / sqrt(40) = 1.4 / 6.3249 = 0.2215 approx. But maybe they want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? Actually the null hypothesis test uses the population mean 98.6. But the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under null is still sigma/sqrt(n). But we don't know population sigma; we use sample sigma as estimate. So answer ~0.2215.

Alternatively, maybe they want the standard deviation of the null distribution of the test statistic? For a t-test, the test statistic t = (sample_mean - population_mean) / (sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size)). The denominator is the standard error. So the standard deviation of the null distribution of t is sqrt(df/(df-2))? No, t distribution has variance df/(df-2) for df>2. But maybe they want the standard deviation of the null distribution of the sample mean? That is standard error. So answer ~0.2215.

Thus answer: about 0.2215. Provide explanation.
